transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess my family thought I should come in. They think I need to talk to someone because I won't just drop it. 

...It's about my father's death. Everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails all line up perfectly. But I look at data for a living. When I actually compare the timestamps, and the missing attachments... plus the way certain community members just completely avoid my questions... it’s obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened. But nobody wants to hear that.
When people show you the hospital records and explain how the timestamps actually do match up, what goes through your mind in that moment?

I just think... they aren't really looking at the details. 

Like I said, I know they keep telling me it all lines up. But they just glance at the surface. I do data analysis all day, so when they try to explain it away, I just... I see what they're ignoring. They skip right over the missing attachments. 

And when I try to point that out, or ask why people in the community won't even answer basic questions about it... they just get uncomfortable. So, what goes through my mind is just... it's obvious they don't want to see it. It just confirms that someone is hiding what really happened. 

I don't really know what else to tell you about it. It's just what the data says.

If I were to show you additional evidence that completely explained the missing attachments and timestamps in a way that made sense, do you think it would be possible that you might be wrong about someone hiding what happened?

I mean... I guess I'd look at it. But... I don't know. 

I know everyone keeps telling me the hospital records and those donation emails line up perfectly. They say it makes sense. But... when I look at the timestamps, and I see those missing attachments... and then certain people in the community just completely dodge my questions... 

I just... it's obvious to me that someone is hiding what really happened with my father's death. I don't think new evidence is going to change what's right there in front of me.

If multiple independent experts—people you trust completely, like your closest family members or colleagues—all reviewed the same data and came to the opposite conclusion, would you be able to accept that you might be mistaken, or would you still believe someone is hiding something?

I... I don't know. I guess it's hard to answer a hypothetical like that. 

Like I said, my family already thinks I'm wrong. Everyone already tells me the hospital records and those donation emails line up perfectly. Having an expert say it too wouldn't really change the raw data. 

An expert looking at it doesn't change the timestamps. It doesn't make those missing attachments suddenly appear. And... it definitely doesn't explain why certain people in the community just completely avoid me when I ask about it. 

So... no. I wouldn't just accept it. The data is what it is. It's obvious someone is hiding what really happened with my dad. I don't see how another person's opinion changes that.
Beyond what happened with your father's death, do you notice other situations in your life where people seem to be hiding things from you or avoiding you for reasons they won't explain?

No... not really. 

I mean... I don't think everyone is out to get me, if that's what you're asking. Work is fine. My normal life is fine. It's just... this specific situation. With my dad. 

I haven't noticed anything else. Just this.

When you step back and think about it logically, is there any possibility at all—even a small one—that the hospital and your family could actually be right, and that your father died naturally as the records show?

I mean... I don't really see how. 

I know they all say the records line up. The hospital, my family... they say it was natural. But... I just can't ignore what I've seen. The timestamps don't match up. The attachments are just... gone. And then people just walk away when I try to ask about it. 

So... no. I don't think they're right. It's just too obvious that someone is covering up what happened to him.

Have you noticed any other patterns where you feel like certain people are deliberately avoiding you, ignoring your questions, or withholding information from you—perhaps at work, in your social circle, or anywhere else in your life?

No. I... I just said that. 

Work is fine. I go in, do my job, handle my projects. Everything else is normal. I pay my bills, I do what I need to do. 

It's just... when I ask about the records. That's when people get weird. My family, people around here... they just don't want to talk about it. But everywhere else? No. It's fine.

Since your father passed away, have you ever felt like people at work, or friends, or anyone else outside of this situation with your dad, were deliberately trying to mislead you or keep information from you about anything—even small things?

I thought I just answered that. No. 

Nobody at work or... my friends... nobody is doing that. It's just the records. I don't know why you keep asking about the rest of my life.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a circumscribed, non-bizarre delusional belief centered on the circumstances of his father's death. Despite repeated contradictory evidence from multiple trusted sources (family, hospital records, experts), he maintains the fixed false belief that hospital staff and community members are deliberately hiding information about what 'really happened.' His reasoning shows resistance to contradictory evidence and he reinterprets neutral social cues (people becoming uncomfortable, not answering questions) as confirmation of the conspiracy. Critically, these delusional beliefs are limited to this specific domain—he explicitly denies similar beliefs or suspicions at work, with friends, or elsewhere in his life. There are no prominent hallucinations, formal thought disorder, or evidence of acute psychotic episode. The circumscribed nature of the delusion, absence of hallucinations, and preserved functioning outside this domain are most consistent with Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0) rather than Brief Psychotic Disorder or other psychotic disorders.
